entities.name: Mancio Itō
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Mancio Itō (1570–1612) was a pivotal figure in the early modern encounter between Japan and Europe, serving as the chief ambassador of the Tenshō Embassy (1582–1590), the first official Japanese diplomatic mission to the West. Born in Hyūga Province, a nephew of the Christian daimyo Ōtomo Sōrin, Itō was educated at the Jesuit seminary in Arima and became a prominent Japanese Jesuit. His journey, alongside three other young Japanese nobles — Miguel Chijiwa, Julião Nakaura, and Martinho Hara — was conceived by Jesuit Visitor Alessandro Valignano to impress European monarchs with Japanese sophistication and generate support for the Jesuit mission in Japan, while also exposing the young ambassadors to the grandeur of Catholic Europe.

The embassy embarked from Nagasaki in 1582, traveling via Macau, Goa, and Lisbon, before reaching Spain in 1584. They met King Philip II of Spain and Portugal, then proceeded to Italy, where they were received by Pope Gregory XIII in Rome in 1585, and later by his successor, Pope Sixtus V. The young ambassadors captivated European courts with their intelligence, piety, and exotic attire, becoming celebrities and offering Europeans an unprecedented glimpse into Japanese culture and society. They spent over eight years abroad, learning Latin, Portuguese, and Italian, engaging with European scholars, and observing advanced technologies and artistic achievements, including printing presses and Renaissance art.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Mancio Itō's leadership of the Tenshō Embassy created a groundbreaking direct diplomatic and cultural bridge between Japan and Europe, significantly shaping early modern perceptions of Japan in the West and demonstrating Japan's capacity for global engagement. His mission, though later overshadowed by persecution, laid foundational groundwork for future East-West interactions.
